caption:
Was a body ever found at Sutton Hoo?

In 1939, under Mound 1 near Woodbridge in Suffolk, practically none of the ship's original timber survived. The form of it did. Stains in the sand had replaced the wood, and nearly all the iron planking rivets sat where they had been driven. Surveyors recorded a vessel 27 metres long, 4.4 metres in the beam, built clinker-fashion with nine planks a side and stiffened by twenty-six wooden ribs. Oar-rests along the gunwales suggest room for forty rowers.

The digging was started by Basil Brown, a self-taught Suffolk archaeologist hired by the landowner Edith Pretty for 30 shillings a week. When national scholars took over, Brown was told to stop. He carried on, which may have saved the site from treasure hunters. A treasure trove inquest ruled the finds belonged to Pretty. She gave them to the nation.

The chamber held a helmet, a sword, a lyre, a great gold buckle with a hidden chamber, shoulder-clasps, and silver plate from the Eastern Roman Empire. The purse held thirty-seven gold coins, each from a different Frankish mint.

Still open: who lay there. No body was found — only a chemical stain, though soil analysis in 1967 detected phosphate, an indicator that a body once rested there. Rædwald of the East Angles has been the favourite candidate since 1940, but one reference work calls the evidence "almost non-existent", and in 2025 Helen Gittos argued for an elite local soldier who had fought for the Byzantine Empire.

Images: the Sutton Hoo helmet photographed in 2016; Mound 1 in 2011; Basil Brown in 1939; Edith Pretty; and a sword-belt end ornament photographed by Gary Todd. All public domain or CC0.
